title: What a devotion is
hook: a personal practice that helps faith, beneath the liturgy

segments.voice: Yesterday, toward unity: Catholics and Orthodox Christians still meeting, still talking across an old split. Your line was one day together. That closes the week, and our time with the Eastern churches. Who did you pray for, East or West? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-two.

Over coffee, a man preparing to become Catholic asks his sponsor a nervous question. Do I have to pray the rosary? And the mercy prayer at three in the afternoon? And wear one of those scapulars? And do the nine-day things? She laughs and says no, none of them. Then she says something that confuses him more: she keeps all of them, and wouldn't give one up. Both answers are true, and the space between them is today's word. For the coming weeks this path walks through the practices that fill Catholic kitchens, purses and parish bulletins. Before the first one, it helps to know what kind of thing they are.
screen: `DO I HAVE TO?` → `NO.` → `BUT SHE KEEPS ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Start at the center. The Second Vatican Council, in its document on the liturgy, calls the liturgy the summit the Church's life climbs toward and the fountain its strength flows from. The Mass and the sacraments are the Church's common prayer, the same words and actions for everyone. Acts gives an early picture of that shared life, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." Now the second layer. Around that center, Catholics have grown a whole garden of other practices: the rosary, the Stations of the Cross, novenas, medals, a picture of the Sacred Heart in the kitchen. The Church calls these devotions, or popular piety. The same council document commends them warmly, and then adds a condition. They should fit the seasons of the Church's year, flow from the liturgy, and lead people back to it. A devotion is a side path that always rejoins the main road. Third, what makes a devotion personal. It's chosen. It often arrives through a person: a grandmother's rosary, a saint met in a book, a prayer card from a funeral. Luke shows Mary doing something like this after the shepherds leave: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Nobody assigned her that. She kept something and turned it over, quietly. Last, the care the Catechism asks for. Popular piety, it says, is a real richness, and it needs the Church's guidance and discernment so that it stays rooted in the faith. A devotion helps when it carries a person toward God and toward other people. It stops helping when it turns into a box to tick, or a way of bargaining. Optional doesn't mean minor. Some people carry one small practice through an illness or a long night in a hospital corridor.
screen: `THE LITURGY: SUMMIT AND FOUNTAIN.` · `DEVOTIONS GROW AROUND IT.` · `CHOSEN, OFTEN HANDED ON.` · `GUIDED, SO IT LEADS BACK.` · then, large: `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one to try. Let your shoulders drop. Let a few devotions pass through your mind without picking yet: beads in a pocket, a quiet minute at three in the afternoon, a candle in front of an image, nine days of praying for one person, a small medal on a chain. Maybe one already lives in your family. Notice which one you lean toward. Just choose one to try once in the coming days, and let the others go. If you pray, you can offer that small choice to God. If you don't, simply hold it as something you'd like to understand from the inside. The bell holds the time.
Devotion. A practice of prayer, freely chosen, that grows around the Church's shared worship and leads back into it. Never required, and often handed down. Today's word.
Your line: optional, and loved. Today, ask someone who keeps a devotion what it is and why they keep it. Then just listen. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Catholics take part in the Church's shared liturgy, above all the Mass, and alongside it some keep personal devotions such as the rosary, novenas, the Stations of the Cross or wearing a blessed medal; these are encouraged but never required.

fork.setup: you're the sponsor. the man asks whether he has to wear a scapular and pray novenas to be Catholic. what's the Church's answer?
options: no: devotions are chosen, not required.
only the ones his parish prefers.
fork.reveal: devotions are optional. the Church commends them and guides them, and she still keeps all of hers.

original.note: Latin: devotion, dedication. Thomas Aquinas describes it as a will ready to give itself to the things of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: devotion just means being very religious.
what it means: a freely chosen practice, like the rosary or a novena, that grows around the liturgy and leads back to it.
what a scholar hears: Sacrosanctum Concilium 13: popular devotions are commended, and should harmonize with the liturgical seasons, derive from the liturgy and lead people to it.
